Is \(\forall x\ \exists y,\ y > x\) the same as \(\exists y\ \forall x,\ y > x\)?
column2: No. The first is true (take y = x + 1). The second claims one number beats every number, which is false. Quantifier order matters.

column1: Read a multi-quantifier statement as a game. Who picks what?
column2: The challenger picks every object behind a for every. You pick every object behind a there exists. Your pick can depend only on choices to its left.

column1: Where is the error in the fake proof that 2 = 1?
column2: It divides both sides by \(a - b\), which equals 0 because a = b.

column1: Does checking 39 cases prove a for-every claim?
column2: No. \(n^2 + n + 41\) is prime for n = 1 to 39 and fails at n = 40: \(1681 = 41^2\).

column1: Five steps to read a proof
column2: Name hypothesis and conclusion. Write every definition. Try small examples. Justify each line. Find the line where the hypothesis does real work.
